text: TPP binding region are fully conserved among HACS and OXC variants, as expected, but much less conserved residues are observed in the formyl-CoA binding and C-terminal regions. Residues uniquely conserved among active variants (RuHACS, ApbHACS and DhcHACS) were chosen for further analysis to understand their catalytic roles. These included three residues from the TPP binding region (H80, Q113 and Y367), four from the formyl-CoA binding region (F112, V354, M392, T397) and seven from the conserved motif at the C-terminal tail of DhcHACS (R541, K542, P543, Q544, Q545, F546, and W548). We used alanine scanning to assess the importance of these residues for catalytic function and stability. The results show that Q113 and Y367 from TPP binding, F112 and M392 from formyl-CoA binding, and F546 and W548 from the C-terminal end region are important for the HACS-catalyzed acyloin condensation between formaldehyde and formyl-CoA (Figure 27). From the analysis of AcHACS crystal structure, the Q residue in the position of DhcHACS Q113 was reported to have a key catalytic function (Berthold, C. L. et al., 2017). Also, a similar impact from the mutations on corresponding residues of F112 and Q113 was observed for RuHACS (Chou, A. et al., 2019). Based on the MSA, OXC variants, including EcOXC, OfOXC, and MeOXC have conserved “Tyrosine- glutamic acid (YE)” residues in the place of FQ (Figure 27). Notably, first-round HACS variants with YE instead of FQ residues (HACS-1-4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11) are clustered together with OXCs in the phylogenetic tree (highlighted in red in Figure 27d). Taken together, FQ and YE could be key characteristic residues that distinguish HACS from OXC. Interestingly, the two additional residues (Y367 and M392) were found to be important for activity (Figure 27B) are also only conserved among HACS but not OXC. 39 Figure 27. Identification of key active site residues of DhcHACS via alanine scanning and rational engineering of DhcHACS using ApbHACS as a template. (A) Active site of DhcHACS with residues that are identified to have catalytic functions via alanine scanning. The red box indicates the catalytic site. (B) Alanine scanning result of six identified residues. Activities represented by the GA flux under resting-cell bioconversion. (C) Activities of “ApbHACS- like” DhcHACS mutants represented by the GA flux under in vivo bioconversion. Bars are drawn at the mean of triplicate biological replicates with error bars representing the standard deviation. All mutants are higher than DhcHACS wildtype (WT) with statistical significance based on Student’s t-test (*p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, and ****p < 0.0001). From the conserved C-terminal motif (RKPQQF-W) among active variants, none of the single mutations completely abolished the activity. This could be because the C-terminal tail of HACS serves as a closing-loop stabilizing substrate (formyl-CoA) binding without exerting a catalytic function. Alanine substitution of the last two residues, F546A and W548A, showed considerable impact on the activity, suggesting the importance of the C-terminal tail (Figure 27B).
